L97: For our cryptographic purposes, it is useful to distinguish a subset $\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{pub}}$ of $\mathcal{F}$, made of public function symbols, that is, intuitively, the symbols made available to the attacker. A recipe (or second-order term) $M$, $N$, $M_{1}$… is a term in ${\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{pub}}[\mathcal{W}\cup\mathcal{X}]}$, that is, a term containing no private (non-public) function symbols.
L98: A plain term (or first-order term) $t$, $r$, $s$, $t_{1}$… is a term in $\mathcal{F}[\mathcal{X}]$, that is, containing no parameters. A (public, ground, non-necessarily linear) $n$-ary context $C$ is a recipe in $\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{pub}}[\mathsf{w}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{w}_{n}]$, where we assume a fixed countable subset of parameters $\{\mathsf{w}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{w}_{n},\ldots\}\subseteq\mathcal{W}$.
L99: If $C$ is a $n$-ary context, $C[T_{1},\ldots,T_{n}]$ denotes the term obtained by replacing each occurrence of $\mathsf{w}_{i}$ with $T_{i}$ in $C$.
L100: ### 2.2 Rewriting
L101: A rewrite system $\mathcal{R}$ is a finite set of rewrite rules ${l\to r}$ where ${l,r\in\mathcal{F}[\mathcal{X}]}$ and such that ${\operatorname{var}(r)\subseteq\operatorname{var}(l)}$. A term $S$ rewrites to $T$ by $\mathcal{R}$, denoted ${S\to_{\mathcal{R}}T}$, if there exist ${l\to r}$ in $\mathcal{R}$, ${p\in\operatorname{pos}(S)}$ and a substitution $\sigma$ such that ${S|_{p}=l\sigma}$ and ${T=S[r\sigma]_{p}}$.
L133: A deduction fact is a pair, written $M\rhd t$, made of a recipe $M\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{pub}}[\mathcal{W}\cup\mathcal{X}]$ and a plain term $t\in\mathcal{F}[\mathcal{X}]$. Such a deduction fact is ground if $\operatorname{var}(M,t)=\emptyset$. A frame, denoted by letters $\varphi$, $\Phi$, $\Phi_{0}$…, is a finite set of ground deduction facts. The image of a frame is defined by $\operatorname{im}(\Phi)=\{t\mid M\rhd t\in\Phi\}$.

L141: ###### Definition 3.1 (Deducibility).
L142: 
L143: Let $\phi$ be finite set of deductions facts. We say that $M$ is a recipe of $t$ in $\phi$, written $M\rhd_{\phi}t$, if there exist a (public, ground, non-necessarily linear) $n$-ary context $C$ and some deduction facts $M_{1}\rhd t_{1}$, …, $M_{n}\rhd t_{n}$ in $\phi$ such that $M=C[M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}]$ and $t=C[t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}]$. In that case, we say that $t$ is syntactically deducible from $\phi$, also written $\phi\vdash t$.
L144: We say that $M$ is a recipe of $t$ in $\phi$ modulo $\mathsf{E}$, written $M\rhd^{\mathsf{E}}_{\phi}t$, if there exists a term $t^{\prime}$ such that $M\rhd_{\phi}t^{\prime}$ and $t^{\prime}=_{\mathsf{E}}t$. In that case, we say that $t$ is deducible from $\phi$ modulo $\mathsf{E}$, written $\phi\vdash_{\mathsf{E}}t$.
L145: We note that $M\rhd_{\varphi}t$ is equivalent to $M\varphi=t$ when $\varphi$ is an initial frame and when $t$ (or equivalently $M$) is ground. We also note that in the case of a frame $\varphi$, since our contexts $C$ are ground and public, $M\rhd_{\varphi}t$ implies $\operatorname{var}(M,t)=\emptyset$ and $\operatorname{par}(M)\subseteq\operatorname{par}(\varphi)$.
L146: ###### Example 3.2.
L147: Consider the equational theory $\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}$ described in Example 【55†2.1】. Let $\varphi_{0}=\{\mathsf{w}_{1}\rhd\mathsf{enc}(\mathsf{c}_{0},\mathsf{k}),\mathsf{w}_{2}\rhd\mathsf{k}\}$ where $\mathsf{c}_{0}$ is a public constant and $\mathsf{k}$ is a private constant. We have that $\varphi_{0}$ is a set of deduction facts. Since, these facts are ground, $\varphi_{0}$ is actually a frame. Moreover, this frame is initial.

L284: Property (【59†a】) ensures that the rules transform a state into a state (and more precisely that the resulting frame in (A.2) is still one-to-one). L285: A simple choice for $\operatorname{Ctx}(\phi\vdash^{?}_{\mathcal{R}}t)$ is to solve the deducibility problem $\phi\vdash^{?}t\mathord{\downarrow}_{\mathcal{R}}$ in the empty equational theory, and then return a corresponding recipe $M$, if any. (This problem is easily solved by induction on $t\mathord{\downarrow}_{\mathcal{R}}$.) We will see in Section 【21†6】 that this choice is sufficient to avoid failure for a large class of equational theories, namely the class of layered convergent theories.

L302: ### 4.3 Main theorem
L303: 
L304: We now state the soundness and the completeness of the transformation rules provided that a saturated state is reached, that is, a state $S\neq\bot$ such that $S\Longrightarrow S^{\prime}$ implies $S^{\prime}=S$. The technical lemmas involved in the proof of this theorem are detailed in Section 【17†5】.
L305: ###### Theorem 4.6 (soundness and completeness)
L306: Let $\mathsf{E}$ be an equational theory generated by a convergent rewrite system $\mathcal{R}$. Let $\varphi$ be an initial frame and $(\Phi,\Psi)$ be a saturated state such that $\operatorname{Init}(\varphi)\Longrightarrow^{*}(\Phi,\Psi)$. 1.
L307: For all $M\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{pub}}[\operatorname{par}(\varphi)]$ and $t\in\mathcal{F}[\emptyset]$, we have that: $$M\varphi=_{\mathsf{E}}t\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\exists N\text{ such that }\Psi\models M\bowtie N\text{ and }N\rhd_{\Phi}t\mathord{\downarrow}_{\mathcal{R}}.$$ 2. For all $M$, $N\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{pub}}[\operatorname{par}(\varphi)\cup\mathcal{X}]$, we have that: $$M\varphi=_{\mathsf{E}}N\varphi\,\Leftrightarrow\,\Psi\models M\bowtie N.$$
L308: We note that this theorem applies to any saturated state reachable from the initial frame. Moreover, while the saturation procedure is sound and complete, it may not terminate, or it may fail if rule A.3 becomes the only applicable rule at some point of computation. In Section 【21†6】 and Section 【25†7】, we explore several sufficient conditions to prevent failure and ensure termination.
L309: ### 4.4 Application to deduction and static equivalence
L310: 
L311: Decision procedures for deduction and static equivalence modulo $\mathsf{E}$ follow from Theorem 【62†4.6】.
L312: #### Algorithm for deduction
L313: 
L314: Let $\varphi$ be an initial frame and $t$ be a ground term. The procedure for checking $\varphi\vdash_{\mathsf{E}}t$ runs as follows:
L315: 
L316:   1. 1.
L317: 
L318: Apply the transformation rules to obtain (if any) a saturated state $(\Phi,\Psi)$ such that $\operatorname{Init}(\varphi)\Longrightarrow^{*}(\Phi,\Psi)$;
L319: 
L320:   2. 2.
L321: Return yes if there exists $N$ such that $N\rhd_{\Phi}t\mathord{\downarrow}_{\mathcal{R}}$ (that is, the $\mathcal{R}$-reduced form of $t$ is syntactically deducible from $\Phi$); otherwise return no.
L322: ###### Proof.
L323: 
L324: If the algorithm returns yes, this means that there exists $N$ such that $N\rhd_{\Phi}t\mathord{\downarrow}_{\mathcal{R}}$. Thanks to Theorem 【62†4.6】 (1), we have that $N\varphi=_{\mathsf{E}}t$, i.e. $N\rhd_{\varphi}^{\mathsf{E}}t$.
L325: 
L326: Conversely, if $t$ is deducible from $\varphi$, then there exists $M$ such that $M\varphi=_{\mathsf{E}}t$. By Theorem 【62†4.6】 (1), there exists $N$ such that $N\rhd_{\Phi}t\mathord{\downarrow}_{\mathcal{R}}$. The algorithm returns yes. ∎∎

L328: 
L329: Consider the frame $\varphi_{0}=\{\mathsf{w}_{1}\rhd\mathsf{enc}(\mathsf{c}_{0},\mathsf{k}),\mathsf{w}_{2}\rhd\mathsf{k}\}$ introduced in Example 【63†3.2】 and let $t_{1}=\langle\mathsf{k},\mathsf{k}\rangle$ and $t_{2}=\mathsf{c}_{0}$. Let $(\Phi_{0},\Psi_{0})$ be the saturated state described in Example 【64†4.4】. We have that:

L331: 
L332: Then, it is easy to see that our algorithm for deduction will return yes for both terms $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$. Indeed, those terms are syntactically deducible from $\varphi_{0}$.
L333: #### Algorithm for static equivalence
L334: 
L335: Let $\varphi_{1}$ and $\varphi_{2}$ be two initial frames. The procedure for checking $\varphi_{1}\approx_{\mathsf{E}}\varphi_{2}$ runs as follows:
L336: 
L337:   1. 1.
L338: 
L339: Apply the transformation rules to obtain (if possible) two saturated states $(\Phi_{1},\Psi_{1})$ and $(\Phi_{2},\Psi_{2})$ such that $\operatorname{Init}(\varphi_{i})\Longrightarrow^{*}(\Phi_{i},\Psi_{i})$, ${i=1,2}$;
L340: 
L341:   2. 2.
L342: For $\{i,j\}=\{1,2\}$, for every equation $(\forall z_{1},\ldots,z_{\ell}.M\bowtie N)$ in $\Psi_{i}$, check that $M\varphi_{j}=_{\mathsf{E}}N\varphi_{j}$ — that is, in other words, $(M\varphi_{j})\mathord{\downarrow}_{\mathcal{R}}=(N\varphi_{j})\mathord{\downarrow}_{\mathcal{R}}$;
L343: 
L344:   3. 3.
L345: 
L346: If so return yes; otherwise return no.
L347: ###### Proof.
L348: If the algorithm returns yes, this means that $M\varphi_{2}=_{\mathsf{E}}N\varphi_{2}$ for every equation $(\forall z_{1},\ldots,z_{\ell}.M\bowtie N)$ in $\Psi_{1}$. Let $M\bowtie N\in\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{1})$. By definition of $\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{1})$, we have that $M\varphi_{1}=_{\mathsf{E}}N\varphi_{1}$. Thanks to Theorem 【62†4.6】 (2), we have that $\Psi_{1}\models M\bowtie N$.
L349: As all the equations in $\Psi_{1}$ are satisfied by $\varphi_{2}$ modulo $\mathsf{E}$, we deduce that $M\varphi_{2}=_{\mathsf{E}}N\varphi_{2}$, i.e. $M\bowtie N\in\operatorname{eq}(\varphi_{2})$. The other inclusion, $\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{2})\subseteq\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{1})$, is proved in the same way.
L350: Conversely, assume now that $\varphi_{1}\approx_{\mathsf{E}}\varphi_{2}$, i.e. $\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{1})=\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{2})$. Consider a quantified equation $\forall z_{1},\ldots,z_{\ell}.M\bowtie N$ in $\Psi_{1}$ and let us show that $M\varphi_{2}=_{\mathsf{E}}N\varphi_{2}$.
L351: (The other case is done in a similar way, and we will conclude that the algorithm returns yes.) Let $\mathsf{c}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{c}_{\ell}$ be free public constants not occurring in $M$ and $N$, and let $(M^{\prime},N^{\prime})=(M,N)\{z_{1}\mapsto\mathsf{c}_{1},\ldots,z_{\ell}\mapsto\mathsf{c}_{\ell}\}$. Since $\Psi_{1}\models M^{\prime}\bowtie N^{\prime}$, by Theorem 【62†4.6】 (2), we have that $M^{\prime}\varphi_{1}=_{\mathsf{E}}N^{\prime}\varphi_{1}$.
L352: Besides, $M^{\prime}$ and $N^{\prime}$ are ground and $\operatorname{par}(M^{\prime},N^{\prime})\subseteq\operatorname{par}(\Psi_{1})\subseteq\operatorname{par}(\varphi_{1})$. Thus, $(M^{\prime}\bowtie N^{\prime})\in\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{1})\subseteq\operatorname{eq}_{\mathsf{E}}(\varphi_{2})$ and $M^{\prime}\varphi_{2}=_{\mathsf{E}}N^{\prime}\varphi_{2}$.
L353: As the constants $\mathsf{c}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{c}_{\ell}$ are free in $\mathsf{E}$ and do not occur in $M$ and $N$, by replacement, we obtain that $M\varphi_{2}=_{\mathsf{E}}N\varphi_{2}$. ∎∎

L357:  | $$(\mathsf{dec}(\mathsf{w}_{1},\mathsf{w}_{2})\varphi_{1}=_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}}\mathsf{c}_{1}\not=_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{enc}}}\mathsf{c}_{0}=\mathsf{c}_{0}\varphi_{1}.$$  |

L441: ## 6 CLTL register-bounded synthesis with partial observation
L442: 
L443: Partial observation aims to improve the modeling capabilities. While a system may contain numerous variables, the controller usually has access to only a few of them [【54†19】]. In this section, we study an extension of $\mathrm{𝖢𝖫𝖳𝖫}$ that features partial observation: we split our set of input variables into two subsets, public (visible) inputs ${𝕀}_{v}$ and private (hidden) inputs ${𝕀}_{h}$.
